name: Flaw Pattern Practice Set
source: Original LR questions written for LSAT Trainer, five per flaw pattern at difficulty 2–5, in the style of PrepTests 150–159. Not LSAC material. MIT licensed.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Term Shift, False Choice, Circular, Straw Man

questions.stimulus: League commissioner: Some fans complain that the Northfield Hockey League is no longer competitive, pointing out that the same two clubs have met in the championship final in each of the past five seasons. These fans are wrong. Our clubs now compete harder than ever for the region's best young players, offering contracts and training facilities far beyond anything they offered a decade ago. So the league is more competitive today than it has ever been.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the commissioner's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: dismisses the fans' complaint by questioning their motives rather than by addressing the evidence they cite
infers that the league's games are closely contested from the fact that clubs compete hard to sign players
presumes that what is true of the league's two most successful clubs is true of every club in the league
takes for granted that the clubs offering the largest contracts are the clubs that reached the championship final
treats the fact that the fans have not proven their claim as sufficient reason to reject that claim
questions.explanation: Equivocation: the fans use 'competitive' to mean that the games and standings are closely contested, while the commissioner's evidence shows only that clubs compete hard to sign players. (B) describes the bad inference from one kind of competition to the other. The tempting trap is (C), but the argument never moves from a trait of the top two clubs to the whole league.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The league is more competitive than ever, so the fans' complaint is wrong.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Clubs now compete harder than ever to sign the best young players, with bigger contracts and better facilities.

breakdown.analysis: So what if clubs fight harder over recruits? The fans weren't talking about recruiting. They said the league isn't competitive because the same two clubs reach the final every year: the games and standings are lopsided. The commissioner answers with a different kind of competition: clubs competing in the market for players. Same word, two meanings. It's like saying a spelling bee is 'competitive' because schools compete to host it, when the complaint was that the same kid wins every year. Prephrase: the argument shifts the meaning of 'competitive.' This is equivocation. It's a classic; know it.

choices.note: The commissioner never attacks the fans' motives. He answers them, just with the wrong kind of evidence. This describes ad hominem, which isn't here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The fans say the league isn't competitive, but they're mostly supporters of losing clubs, so we can ignore them.

choices.note: CORRECT. The fans' claim is about how closely contested the games and standings are. The commissioner infers that the league is more competitive from evidence that clubs compete to sign players. That's a different kind of competition, so the inference rides on two meanings of one word.

Tempting, because the two finalist clubs are mentioned. But the argument draws no conclusion about every club from the top two. Its evidence is about all clubs' recruiting; the problem is what kind of competition that evidence shows.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our two best clubs have excellent coaches, so every club in the league has excellent coaches.

choices.note: The argument doesn't need this and doesn't assume it. Which clubs pay the most has nothing to do with the commissioner's reasoning.
The commissioner cites positive evidence (bigger contracts, better facilities); he doesn't rely on the fans' failure to prove anything. Wrong flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the league is uncompetitive, so it must be competitive.

questions.stimulus: Wheat farmers in the arid Pellan Basin lose much of their harvest whenever rainfall is low. The new wheat variety Tamsk-4 has just been certified as drought-tolerant by the national seed board after three years of field trials. Therefore, Pellan Basin farmers who switch to Tamsk-4 can expect to harvest considerably more wheat in dry years than they now do.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: In years of normal rainfall, Tamsk-4 yields about as much grain as the varieties now grown in the basin.
Some farmers in the Pellan Basin already irrigate part of their wheat fields during years of low rainfall.
Tamsk-4 seed costs somewhat more per acre than the seed that most Pellan Basin farmers currently plant.
The seed board certifies a variety as drought-tolerant if its plants survive prolonged drought, however little grain they produce.
Several wheat varieties that the seed board certified as drought-tolerant in the past are no longer widely planted.
questions.explanation: The argument slides from 'drought-tolerant' in the seed board's sense to 'produces a good harvest in drought.' (D) shows the board's term means only that the plants survive, so certification says nothing about yield, which is what the conclusion is about. (E) is tempting, but varieties can fall out of use for many reasons (price, taste, disease), so it does not show Tamsk-4 will fail to raise dry-year harvests.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Farmers who switch to Tamsk-4 will harvest considerably more wheat in dry years.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Pellan farmers lose much of their harvest in dry years; Tamsk-4 is certified 'drought-tolerant' by the seed board.

breakdown.analysis: What does 'drought-tolerant' actually mean here? The conclusion is about harvest: more grain in dry years. The evidence is a label. If the label means 'the plant stays alive,' a field of living but nearly empty wheat plants would qualify. Prephrase: we want something showing the certification isn't about grain yield. It's like buying a 'waterproof' watch to go diving when 'waterproof' on the box only means it survives rain. Watch for weakeners that attack the meaning of a key term rather than the conclusion head-on.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument is about dry years. Matching yields in normal years says nothing about drought performance.
So? Some farmers irrigating part of their fields doesn't tell us whether Tamsk-4 will raise dry-year harvests. If anything, the rest still need help.
Wrong dimension. The conclusion is about how much wheat farmers will harvest, not whether switching is worth the money.
CORRECT. The board's 'drought-tolerant' means the plants survive, not that they produce grain. The conclusion needs the second meaning, so the certification no longer supports it.
Tempting, because it hints that certification hasn't worked before. But varieties drop out of use for lots of reasons: cost, disease, taste, a newer variety. Merely possible isn't enough to weaken.

questions.stimulus: The county's preservation ordinance requires that any building listed as historic by the county be preserved. The old Delmore grain elevator is unquestionably historic: it was the site of the 1931 farmers' strike, one of the most important events in the county's past. Therefore, the Delmore grain elevator must be preserved.
questions.stem: Which one of the following contains a pattern of flawed reasoning most similar to that in the argument above?
choices: The library's rules allow any registered member to borrow rare books. Mr. Kato is clearly a member of the library's community, having volunteered there for years. Therefore, Mr. Kato is allowed to borrow rare books.

Every employee whom the company designates as essential must report to work during storms. Raj's supervisor has formally designated Raj as essential. Therefore, Raj must report to work during the coming storm.
Every ingredient in the stew that Mia brought to the county fair is certified organic by the state agriculture board. Therefore, Mia's stew is itself certified organic by the state agriculture board.

Any athlete named to the all-star team receives a bonus from the league. Dara was named player of the week three times this season, more often than anyone else. Therefore, Dara will receive a bonus from the league.

Every vehicle registered as commercial must pay the toll on the Harbor Street bridge. Ana's van paid the toll on that bridge this morning. Therefore, Ana's van must be registered with the state as commercial.
questions.explanation: The ordinance covers buildings that are officially 'listed as historic,' but the argument shows only that the elevator is historic in the everyday sense of historically important, an equivocation. (A) does the same thing with 'member': the rule covers registered members, and the argument shows only that Kato is a member of the community. (D) is the tempting trap because it also fails to show the official status, but it never trades on two senses of one term; it simply offers evidence of a different honor.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Delmore grain elevator must be preserved.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Buildings listed as historic by the county must be preserved; the elevator is historic because an important event happened there.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: A rule applies to things with an official status called X; this thing is X in the everyday sense; so the rule applies.

breakdown.analysis: Is the elevator 'listed as historic'? We're never told. We're told it's historic in the ordinary sense: something important happened there. The argument uses one word in two senses: official listing and real-world importance. Prephrase: find a rule about an official category, a case that fits the everyday meaning of the same word, and a conclusion that the rule applies. Lesson: in parallel-flaw questions, match the flaw itself, not just the topic or the presence of a rule.

choices.note: CORRECT. The rule covers 'registered members.' Kato is a 'member' only in the everyday sense of belonging to the library's community. Same word, two senses, rule wrongly applied, exactly like 'historic.' Note the rule's direction matches too: registered member → may borrow, just as listed historic → must be preserved.
This one is valid. Raj really has the official status, so the rule applies. A good parallel-flaw answer has to be flawed.
A part-to-whole flaw: certification of each ingredient doesn't automatically certify the dish. Different flaw.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Every brick in the wall is light, so the wall is light.

choices.note: Tempting, because it also fails to show the official status (named to the all-star team). But it doesn't use one term in two senses; it just offers a different honor as if it were the required one. The stimulus's error is the double meaning of 'historic.'
This is a different flaw: it reverses a conditional. Commercial → pays toll; pays toll, so commercial. No word shifts meaning.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All cats have whiskers. My pet has whiskers. So my pet is a cat.

questions.stimulus: Nursing administrator: State regulations require that every hospital unit have, on each shift, at least one nurse who is certified in critical care. Critics charge that our cardiac unit violated this rule last month, since on several night shifts the only nurse present with critical-care training had allowed her certificate to lapse. But her training was every bit as thorough as that of any certified nurse. So the unit complied with the regulation.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the administrator's argument?
choices: The nurse whose certificate had lapsed was the most experienced nurse working on any of the cardiac unit's night shifts last month.
The critics would not have objected to the staffing of the cardiac unit if the nurse's certificate had been current.
No other unit in the hospital went through a shift last month without a nurse certified in critical care.
Nurses whose critical-care certificates have lapsed generally provide care as good as that provided by nurses whose certificates are current.
The regulation's requirement of critical-care certification can be met by a nurse who is fully trained but whose certificate has lapsed.
questions.explanation: The regulation requires a nurse who is 'certified,' but the administrator shows only that the nurse was as well trained as a certified nurse; the argument needs 'certified' to mean merely 'trained to that standard.' (E) states this, and if it is false, the unit did not comply. (D) is tempting, but the conclusion is about compliance with the rule, not quality of care; even if lapsed nurses generally gave worse care, this particular nurse's training could still satisfy the rule if (E) is true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The cardiac unit complied with the regulation.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The rule requires a nurse certified in critical care on each shift; on some shifts the only trained nurse had a lapsed certificate; her training was as thorough as any certified nurse's.

breakdown.analysis: Does 'certified' mean 'holds a current certificate' or just 'has the training'? The critics read it the first way, and that's the natural reading. The administrator wins only if the rule's 'certified' can be satisfied by training alone. Prephrase: the regulation counts a trained nurse with a lapsed certificate as meeting the requirement. It's like saying you have a valid driver's license because you drive as well as anyone with a license. Watch for an equivocation on the key term of the rule.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The argument doesn't need her to be the most experienced; it needs her to satisfy the rule. Negating it changes nothing.
choices.negation: The nurse whose certificate had lapsed was not the most experienced nurse working on the cardiac unit's night shifts last month.

choices.note: The critics' hypothetical reactions don't matter. Negating it doesn't touch whether the unit complied.
choices.negation: The critics would have objected even if the nurse's certificate had been current.

choices.note: Other units are out of scope. The conclusion is only about the cardiac unit.
choices.negation: Some other unit in the hospital went through a shift last month without a nurse certified in critical care.

choices.note: Tempting, since it sounds like the administrator's point. But the conclusion is about compliance, not care quality, and it's about this nurse, not lapsed nurses 'generally.' Negate it and her own training can still be thorough; the argument stands or falls on what the rule means.
choices.negation: Nurses whose certificates have lapsed generally do not provide care as good as that of nurses with current certificates.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the requirement cannot be met by a fully trained nurse whose certificate has lapsed. Then the unit violated the rule on those shifts, and the argument collapses.
choices.negation: The regulation's requirement of critical-care certification cannot be met by a nurse who is fully trained but whose certificate has lapsed.

questions.stimulus: Media critic: The Ridgeport Courier describes itself on its masthead as an independent newspaper, a term papers have long used to signal that they are not affiliated with any political party. Yet the Courier is owned by a corporation with large holdings in real estate and broadcasting, and a newspaper whose owner has such commercial interests cannot be independent of those interests. Thus, the Courier's description of itself is inaccurate.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the media critic's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: presumes, without providing justification, that a corporation's commercial interests will shape what its newspaper chooses to report
attributes to the newspaper a characteristic that properly belongs only to the corporation that owns it
takes for granted that the newspaper, in calling itself independent, was claiming to be free of commercial interests
attacks the newspaper's credibility by pointing to its owner's business interests rather than to the content of its reporting
concludes that the newspaper is affiliated with a political party merely because it is not free of commercial interests
questions.explanation: The Courier calls itself 'independent' in the sense of having no party affiliation; the critic shows it is not independent in a different sense (free of commercial interests) and concludes the Courier's claim is false. That works only if the Courier was claiming commercial independence, which (C) says the critic takes for granted. (B) is the most tempting trap because the critic moves from the owner to the paper, but the critic gives a reason for that move; the real problem is that the claim the paper actually made could still be true.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Courier's description of itself as 'independent' is inaccurate.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Papers use 'independent' to mean not affiliated with a political party; the Courier's owner has big commercial interests; a paper with such an owner can't be independent of those interests.

breakdown.analysis: Independent of what? The critic tells us exactly what the Courier means: no political party. Then the critic proves something else: the paper isn't independent of its owner's business interests. Both can be true at once. A paper can be party-free and still tied to real estate money. Prephrase: the critic refutes a claim the Courier never made by switching what 'independent' means. It's like calling a restaurant's 'fresh' fish a lie because the chef isn't fresh out of culinary school. Lesson: when an argument says someone's claim is false, check that it uses their meaning.

choices.note: Tempting, because it sounds like a fair complaint about media ownership. But the critic never says the interests shape the reporting; the premise is only that the paper can't be independent of them. And even granting it, the Courier's actual claim (no party ties) survives.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The paper is owned by a developer, so its housing stories must be slanted toward developers.

choices.note: Tempting, because the argument moves from owner to paper. But the critic offers a premise linking them (a paper with such an owner can't be independent of those interests). That's not a bare part/whole slip. The killer problem is the meaning shift.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The corporation that owns the paper is huge, so the paper must be huge.

choices.note: CORRECT. The Courier used 'independent' in its long-standing sense: no party affiliation. The critic's conclusion follows only if the Courier was claiming freedom from commercial interests, and the critic simply takes that for granted. Refuting the second meaning doesn't touch the claim the Courier actually made.
The critic isn't attacking credibility or saying the reporting is untrustworthy; the critic is disputing a self-description. Ad hominem doesn't fit.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Don't trust the Courier's stories; its owner is a real estate tycoon.

choices.note: The critic never concludes that the paper has party ties. The conclusion is only that the description is inaccurate. This misdescribes the argument.

questions.stimulus: Sales of the Brisa coffee maker have fallen for two straight years, while competing manufacturers have cut their prices on comparable models by nearly a third. So the Brisa's maker must either lower the Brisa's price to match its competitors' prices or stop producing it altogether. Since lowering the price that much would make the Brisa unprofitable, the company should discontinue it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: relies on the competitors' pricing decisions as evidence about the quality of the company's coffee maker
fails to establish that the coffee maker's sales have fallen faster than the sales of its competitors' comparable models
concludes that the coffee maker is already unprofitable merely because its sales have fallen for two straight years
presumes that what is true of the company's coffee maker is true of every product that the company makes
fails to consider that the coffee maker's sales might be revived by some means other than a price cut
questions.explanation: False dichotomy: the argument treats 'cut the price' and 'discontinue' as the only options, ignoring others such as improving the product or advertising it differently. (E) says so. (C) is tempting, but the argument never says the Brisa is unprofitable now; the claim is that a deep price cut would make it unprofitable.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The company should discontinue the Brisa.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Sales have fallen two years in a row; either cut the price to match competitors or discontinue; cutting the price would make it unprofitable.

breakdown.analysis: Why are those the only two choices? The company could redesign the Brisa, advertise it, add features, sell it in new stores, or just keep selling it at lower volume. The argument knocks out option one and declares option two the winner. That's a false choice. It's like saying: either I buy a new car or I walk to work; a new car is too expensive, so I'll walk. What about the bus? Prephrase: the argument ignores other options. This flaw (false dichotomy) is a classic; know it.

choices.note: The argument never treats competitors' prices as evidence of quality. It just mentions matching them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our competitors charge more, so their coffee makers must be better.

choices.note: Irrelevant. Whether competitors' sales also fell doesn't affect whether the two options are the only ones.
Tempting, but read carefully. The argument says lowering the price that much would make it unprofitable, not that it's unprofitable now. The argument doesn't draw this conclusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Sales fell, so we must be losing money on this product.

choices.note: The argument is only about the Brisa. Nothing is said about other products.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The Brisa is losing sales, so all our appliances are losing sales.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument treats a price cut and discontinuation as the only options. Other ways to revive sales (redesign, advertising, new stores) are never considered.

questions.stimulus: Last March the faint star Orvel-12 brightened tenfold for about two days and then returned to normal. A brightening like this can result from a flare on the star's surface or from gravitational lensing, which occurs when a massive object passes between us and the star. Flares change a star's color as it brightens, but Orvel-12's color stayed the same throughout. So the brightening was caused by lensing.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most strengthens the argument?
choices: No process other than a flare or lensing is known to make a star brighten tenfold without changing its color.
Some flares on stars similar to Orvel-12 have lasted considerably longer than two days before the star dimmed again.
Most of the stars that astronomers have seen brighten tenfold for a few days did so because of flares.
Flares on stars like Orvel-12 typically make the star appear redder rather than bluer as it brightens.
Lensing events involving stars as faint as Orvel-12 are only rarely detected, even by astronomers who search for them.
questions.explanation: The argument eliminates flares and concludes lensing, which works only if those are the only two possible causes; it treats 'can result from' as if it listed every possibility. (A) closes that gap by ruling out other known causes. (C) is tempting because it is about causes of brightening, but it actually makes flares more likely in general and so, if anything, weakens the argument.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Lensing caused Orvel-12's brightening.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Such brightening can come from a flare or from lensing; flares change a star's color; Orvel-12's color didn't change.

breakdown.analysis: Are flares and lensing the only things that can do this? The argument says the brightening 'can result from' either, which isn't the same as 'can only result from' one of them. Knock out flares, and lensing wins only if there's no third suspect. It's like saying the cookies were eaten by the dog or the cat; the cat was locked out, so the dog did it. What about your little brother? Prephrase: we want an answer that rules out other causes. Strengtheners for a false-choice argument usually close the list of options.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument is a process of elimination with only two candidates. This answer confirms there's no known third candidate, so eliminating flares really does point to lensing.
Irrelevant. Flare duration doesn't matter; the argument eliminates flares by color, not by length.
Tempting, because it's about what causes brightening. But it says flares are the usual cause, which pushes against lensing. Wrong direction.
So? Which way flares shift the color doesn't matter. Orvel-12's color didn't change at all.
If anything this hurts: if lensing of faint stars is rarely seen, it's a less likely explanation. It doesn't help.

questions.stimulus: The Fenwick Rovers' poor season must be due either to the departure of their star goalkeeper or to their new coach's defensive system. But the goalkeeper who replaced him has posted statistics nearly identical to his. So the new coach's defensive system is to blame for the Rovers' poor season.
questions.stem: The flawed reasoning in which one of the following is most closely parallel to the flawed reasoning in the argument above?
choices: The bakery's profits began to fall shortly after the new manager was hired and started changing the staff schedule. So the new manager's staffing decisions, and not some other factor, are to blame for the falling profits.
Every ticket to the concert was bought either online or at the box office. But the box office sold no tickets at all for that concert. So every ticket to the concert must have been bought online.

The orchard's poor harvest was due either to the late frost or to the summer drought. Since the late frost clearly damaged the orchard's blossoms, the drought cannot have contributed at all to the orchard's poor harvest.

The bakery's falling profits must be due either to higher flour costs or to the new manager's staffing decisions. But the bakery has paid the same flour price for a year. So the manager's staffing is to blame.
The three Rovers fans interviewed by a local radio station after the final game all blamed the coach for the poor season. So most of the team's fans must blame the coach for the poor season.
questions.explanation: The argument assumes without support that only two causes are possible, rules one out, and blames the other: a false dichotomy. (D) matches step for step. (C) is the strongest trap: it also starts from 'either X or Y,' but it confirms one cause and concludes the other played no part, a different error (treating the 'or' as exclusive). (B) has the same form but its two options really are exhaustive, so it is not flawed.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The new coach's defensive system is to blame.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The poor season was caused either by losing the goalkeeper or by the coach's system; the replacement goalkeeper is just as good.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Effect must be due to X or Y (unjustified list); not X; so Y.

breakdown.analysis: Why only those two causes? Injuries, a tougher schedule, a weaker offense: plenty of other things can wreck a season. The argument rules out one cause and convicts the other. Prephrase: find an argument that sets up an unsupported two-option list for a cause, eliminates one, and blames the other. Watch for look-alikes: same 'either/or' setup but a different move (confirming one and dismissing the other), or a list that really is complete.

choices.note: A timing-based causal flaw (after, therefore because of). No two-option list is set up and eliminated.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The team started losing after the new uniforms arrived, so the uniforms are to blame.

choices.note: Same shape, but no flaw. A ticket really can be bought only online or at the box office (that's given as true of every ticket), so the elimination is valid. The stimulus's list is not justified.
Tempting: it opens with the same 'either X or Y.' But it confirms X and then denies Y, which assumes the two causes can't both contribute. That's a different flaw from eliminating X and blaming Y.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The lawn died from either the heat or the bugs. The heat definitely hurt it, so the bugs didn't.

choices.note: CORRECT. Same skeleton: falling profits must be due to flour costs or staffing (no reason to think those are the only causes); the flour price hasn't changed; so staffing is to blame.
A sampling flaw: three fans can't represent most fans. Different flaw, though it shares the Rovers topic to lure you.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The two shoppers I asked liked the store, so most shoppers like it.

questions.stimulus: The Darrow Creek bridge can no longer safely carry loaded grain trucks. Repairing it would cost $4 million, while replacing it with a new bridge would cost $6 million. A repaired bridge would need major work again within fifteen years, but a new bridge would last at least fifty. Hence, the county should build a new bridge.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the argument depends?
choices: A repaired Darrow Creek bridge would not remain safe for loaded grain trucks for more than ten years.
Permanently barring loaded grain trucks from the bridge would not serve the county better than replacing the bridge.
The county can pay for a new bridge without raising property taxes or cutting other road projects.
Most of the traffic that crosses the Darrow Creek bridge on an ordinary day consists of loaded grain trucks.
A new bridge could be built in no more time than it would take to repair the existing bridge.
questions.explanation: The argument compares only two options, repair and replacement, and picks the better one; the conclusion that the county should build a new bridge requires that no other option, such as closing the bridge to heavy trucks, is better. (B) is the narrow version of that assumption, and negating it defeats the recommendation. (C) is tempting because cost matters, but the argument doesn't need the money to come without a tax increase; a tax-funded bridge could still be the right choice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The county should build a new bridge.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The bridge can't safely carry loaded grain trucks; repair costs $4M and lasts ~15 years; replacement costs $6M and lasts 50+.

breakdown.analysis: Repair vs. replace: is that really the whole menu? The county could also just keep heavy trucks off the bridge and route them another way. Comparing two options can tell you which of the two is better; it can't tell you what the county should do unless no other option beats the winner. Prephrase: the argument assumes there's no better alternative than a new bridge, such as leaving it unrepaired for trucks. It's like deciding to buy the $6 sandwich because it's a better deal than the $4 one, never asking if you should just eat at home. Necessary-assumption tip: negate each answer and see if the argument dies.

choices.note: Not needed. The argument already says a repair needs major work within fifteen years. Whether the safe life is 10 or 14 years doesn't decide anything.
choices.negation: A repaired bridge would remain safe for loaded grain trucks for more than ten years.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: barring grain trucks from the bridge for good would serve the county better than replacing it. Then the recommendation is wrong, even though a new bridge beats a repair.
choices.negation: Permanently barring loaded grain trucks from the bridge would serve the county better than replacing the bridge.

choices.note: Tempting, since money is part of the argument. But negate it: the county would have to raise taxes. The new bridge could still be the right call. The argument isn't about how to pay.
choices.negation: The county cannot pay for a new bridge without raising property taxes or cutting other road projects.

choices.note: Not needed. Even if grain trucks are a minority of traffic, the bridge still has to be dealt with; the argument doesn't depend on traffic shares.
choices.negation: Most of the traffic over the bridge on an ordinary day does not consist of loaded grain trucks.

choices.note: Not needed. A new bridge could take longer to build and still be worth it for its fifty-year life.
choices.negation: A new bridge could not be built in as little time as it would take to repair the existing bridge.

questions.stimulus: Nurse manager: Critics claim that our hospital's practice of rotating nurses among units every six months harms patient care, since rotated nurses lose familiarity with each unit's routines. But in the two years since rotation began, rates of medication errors, patient falls, and readmissions on every unit have remained essentially what they were before. The critics are therefore mistaken, and rotation should be counted among the practices that improve the care our patients receive.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the nurse manager's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: draws a conclusion about the effects of a practice from data gathered over too short a period to be reliable
confuses a correlation between a practice and an outcome with a causal relationship between them
overlooks the possibility that a practice may neither harm patient care nor improve it
presumes, without justification, that the critics' position is based only on anecdotal reports
fails to consider whether rotation has benefits for the nurses who take part in it
questions.explanation: The evidence (outcomes unchanged) does undercut the claim that rotation harms care, but the manager then concludes that rotation improves care, as if 'harms' and 'improves' were the only possibilities; (C) points out the overlooked middle option of no effect. (A) is the most tempting trap, but two years across every unit is not obviously too short, and even with more data the leap from 'no harm' to 'improves' would remain. (B) fails because the data show no change at all, so the manager is not inferring cause from a correlation.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The critics are wrong, and rotation improves patient care.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Critics say rotation harms care; since rotation began, errors, falls, and readmissions have stayed essentially the same.

breakdown.analysis: If nothing changed, how did rotation improve anything? The data do knock out 'rotation harms care.' But the manager doesn't stop there. She jumps to 'rotation improves care,' as if not-harmful means helpful. There's a third option: rotation does nothing either way. This is the polar-opposite trap: 'not bad' isn't 'good.' It's like saying a new diet didn't make you gain weight, so it must be making you lose weight, when the scale hasn't moved. Prephrase: the argument ignores the possibility of no effect.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'too short a period' is a real-sounding flaw. But two years of data on every unit isn't obviously too short, and the argument's big problem would remain even with ten years: unchanged outcomes can't show improvement.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our new hiring rule has been in place for a week and no one has quit, so it has solved our turnover problem.

choices.note: There's no correlation to confuse. Outcomes didn't move. The manager isn't inferring a cause from two things changing together.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Falls dropped after we bought new beds, so the new beds prevented falls.

choices.note: CORRECT. The argument treats 'doesn't harm' as 'improves,' ignoring the in-between possibility that rotation has no effect on care.
The manager doesn't characterize the critics' evidence at all. She states their reason (loss of familiarity) accurately.
Wrong dimension. The argument is about patient care. Benefits to nurses wouldn't fix or reveal the flaw.

questions.stimulus: Newspaper editor: Diners choosing where to eat would do well to consult the Harlan Gazette first, because its restaurant reviews are the most reliable in the city. After all, our critics are the best judges of food in the city. And we know this because their reviews have proven more reliable than anyone else's.
questions.stem: The editor's argument is flawed because it
choices: treats the reliability of the Gazette's reviews as support for a claim offered to support that reliability
relies on the popularity of the Gazette's reviews among diners as evidence that those reviews are accurate
generalizes about all of the Gazette's reviews on the basis of only a few reviews by its critics
fails to specify what it would mean for one restaurant review to be more reliable than another
attacks the competence of rival critics instead of presenting evidence about the quality of the Gazette's own reviews
questions.explanation: Circular reasoning: the reviews are reliable because the critics are the best judges, and the critics are the best judges because their reviews are reliable. (A) describes this loop without naming it. (D) is tempting because 'reliable' is never defined, but an undefined term is not what makes the argument fail; even with a definition, the support would still run in a circle.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Diners should consult the Gazette first, because its restaurant reviews are the most reliable in the city.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Its critics are the best judges of food; we know that because their reviews are the most reliable.

breakdown.analysis: Where's the outside evidence? Trace it: reviews are reliable ← critics are the best judges ← reviews are reliable. The conclusion shows up again as the support for its own premise. That's circular reasoning. It's like saying 'I'm trustworthy because I always tell the truth, and you know I tell the truth because I'm trustworthy.' Prephrase: the argument assumes what it's trying to prove.

choices.note: CORRECT. 'Critics are the best judges' is offered to support the reviews' reliability, but its only support is that same reliability. The argument uses its conclusion to prop up its own premise.
Popularity isn't mentioned. The support is the critics' supposed judgment, not how many people read them.
choices.example: Example of flaw: More people read our reviews than any others, so they must be the most accurate.

choices.note: No sample of reviews is cited at all. That's part of the problem, but it's not a hasty generalization.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our last two reviews were spot on, so all our reviews are reliable.

choices.note: Tempting, because 'reliable' is vague. But defining it wouldn't fix anything: the support would still loop back to the conclusion. Pick the flaw the argument actually commits.
The editor never attacks rival critics. Nothing is said about anyone else's competence.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The Tribune's reviewers are amateurs who can't cook, so our reviews are better.

questions.stimulus: Nurses at Linfield Hospital now use the Corbel Pain Scale, on which patients rate their pain by choosing among a series of drawn faces. This scale accurately measures patients' pain. After all, in a recent study on the hospital's surgical ward, patients' Corbel scores closely matched the pain levels that their nurses assigned them.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption required by the argument?
choices: Patients find the Corbel scale easier to use than the pain scales that the hospital used previously.
Nurses' assessments of patients' pain are more accurate than patients' own descriptions of their pain.
Most of the patients in the study were experiencing at least moderate pain when they were assessed.
The nurses in the study did not base their assessments of patients' pain on the patients' Corbel scores.
No other pain scale has been shown to match nurses' assessments of pain as closely as the Corbel scale does.
questions.explanation: The study validates the Corbel scale by checking it against nurses' assessments; if the nurses simply read off the Corbel scores, the match would be guaranteed and would prove nothing, making the support circular. (D) rules this out. (B) is tempting, but it is too strong: the argument needs nurses' assessments to be a reasonable, independent check, not better than patients' own reports.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Corbel scale accurately measures patients' pain.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: In a study, patients' Corbel scores closely matched the pain levels nurses assigned them.

breakdown.analysis: What if the nurses got their numbers from the Corbel scale? Then the scores would match because they're the same scores, and the 'test' would just check the scale against itself. A match only means something if the two measures are independent. It's like proving your bathroom scale is accurate by noting it agrees with what you wrote down from your bathroom scale. Prephrase: the nurses' ratings weren't derived from the Corbel scores. Necessary-assumption tip: negate each choice and see if the argument breaks.

choices.note: Ease of use is a different question from accuracy. Wrong dimension.
choices.negation: Patients do not find the Corbel scale easier to use than the earlier scales.

choices.note: Too strong. The argument needs the nurses' ratings to be a decent independent check, not better than patients' own reports. Negate it and the argument survives.
choices.negation: Nurses' assessments of pain are not more accurate than patients' own descriptions of their pain.

choices.note: Not needed. A scale can match nurses' judgments across mild pain too. Negating this doesn't hurt.
choices.negation: Most of the patients in the study were not experiencing at least moderate pain.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the nurses based their ratings on the Corbel scores. Then the match is automatic and shows nothing about accuracy. The argument collapses.
choices.negation: The nurses in the study based their assessments of patients' pain on the patients' Corbel scores.

choices.note: Not needed. The conclusion is that Corbel is accurate, not that it's the most accurate. Another scale doing as well wouldn't hurt.
choices.negation: Some other pain scale has been shown to match nurses' assessments as closely as the Corbel scale does.

questions.stimulus: Architect: The Merrow Library is the most successful public building in our city. The success of a public building should be judged by the opinions of people qualified to evaluate architecture. And anyone who fails to see the Merrow Library's superiority to the city's other public buildings plainly lacks such qualifications.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the architect's argument?
choices: Dr. Imre's book is the best history of the region ever written. Every historian who has reviewed the book has praised it highly, and historians are clearly the people best qualified to judge works of history.

The Rialto is the best theater in town. A theater's quality should be judged by how many people choose to attend it, and more people attended performances at the Rialto last year than at any other theater in town.

Most critics of the Merrow Library's design are architects whose own proposals for the library were rejected by the city. So their criticisms are probably motivated by resentment and should not be taken seriously.

Anyone with a discerning palate appreciates Calla's cider, and Jo appreciates Calla's cider more than any other drink. So Jo must have a discerning palate, and her opinions about other ciders deserve our trust.

Calla's cider is the best cider made in the valley. Cider should be judged by people with discerning palates, and anyone who does not prefer Calla's cider to the valley's other ciders obviously lacks a discerning palate.
questions.explanation: The architect defines the qualified judges as exactly those who agree with the conclusion, so the appeal to their judgment assumes what it is meant to prove: circular reasoning. (E) defines discerning judges as those who prefer Calla's cider in the same way. (A) is the strongest trap because it also appeals to qualified judges, but historians are identified independently of whether they praise the book, so its reasoning is not circular.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The Merrow Library is the city's most successful public building.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Success should be judged by qualified people; anyone who doesn't see the library's superiority isn't qualified.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: X is best; judge by qualified judges; anyone who doesn't think X is best isn't qualified.

breakdown.analysis: How do we know who's qualified? By whether they agree the library is best. So 'the qualified judges agree' is guaranteed: anyone who disagrees is thrown out. The conclusion is built into the definition of the judges. That's circular. It's like a contest where the judges are 'everyone who votes for me.' Prephrase: find an argument that appeals to expert judges and then defines the experts as the people who reach the desired conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting, since it also appeals to qualified judges. But historians are qualified for reasons independent of liking this book. That's an ordinary appeal to authority, not a circle.

An appeal to popularity, not circular reasoning. The standard (attendance) is set independently of the conclusion, and the attendance numbers are outside evidence: weak evidence, maybe, but not a loop.
choices.example: Example of flaw: This song is the best of the year because it was streamed the most.

choices.note: An attack on the critics' motives (ad hominem), using the same library to lure you. No circle here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Ignore the senator's tax plan; she's rich.

choices.note: Same cider topic, different flaw: it reverses a conditional. Discerning → appreciates; appreciates, so discerning. No one is defined into agreement.
choices.example: Example of flaw: All doctors know CPR. Sam knows CPR. So Sam is a doctor.

choices.note: CORRECT. Judges with 'discerning palates' are defined as those who prefer Calla's cider, so the appeal to their judgment assumes the conclusion, exactly like the architect's 'qualified' people.

questions.stimulus: The unsigned 1872 editorial in the Corley Sentinel opposing the railroad tax was written by Rhoda Pell, the paper's editor at the time. The editorial contains several unusual turns of phrase, and each of these phrases also appears in at least one of the editorials attributed to Pell in the standard catalogue of her work. No other writer of that period is known to have used these phrases.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Pell was not the only writer at the Sentinel in 1872 who publicly opposed the railroad tax in print.
Some of the editorials that the standard catalogue attributes to Pell contain none of the unusual phrases found in the 1872 editorial.
The catalogue attributes editorials to Pell mainly because they share those phrases with the 1872 editorial, long presumed to be hers.
The Sentinel published unsigned editorials more often in 1872 than in any other year during which Pell edited the paper.
The standard catalogue of Pell's work was compiled more than fifty years after her death by a single scholar.
questions.explanation: The argument treats the catalogue's attributions as independent evidence of Pell's style. (C) shows they were made by presuming the 1872 editorial was hers, so using them to prove that editorial is hers is circular and the match is no evidence at all. (A) is tempting because it names other possible authors, but the argument rests on the phrases, which no other writer is known to have used.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Rhoda Pell wrote the unsigned 1872 editorial.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The editorial's unusual phrases appear in editorials the standard catalogue attributes to Pell; no other writer is known to have used them.

breakdown.analysis: How do we know those catalogue editorials are Pell's? The argument treats them as a known sample of her writing. But if they were credited to Pell because they sound like the 1872 editorial, which was simply assumed to be hers, then the 'match' is a loop: the 1872 piece proves the others, and the others prove the 1872 piece. Prephrase: show the comparison set isn't independent. It's like confirming a rumor by checking with people who heard it from you. Indirect weakeners like this attack the evidence, not the conclusion.

choices.note: Tempting: another tax opponent could have written it. But the argument doesn't rest on Pell's opinion; it rests on her distinctive phrases, which no one else is known to have used. This barely dents it.
Irrelevant. Writers don't use their pet phrases in every piece. The argument only needs each phrase to show up somewhere in her work.
CORRECT. The catalogue's attributions depend on assuming the 1872 editorial was Pell's. So using them to prove it's Pell's is circular, and the phrase match stops being evidence.
So? More unsigned editorials in 1872 doesn't tell us who wrote this one.
Tempting if you think 'old catalogue by one scholar = unreliable.' But a late or single-author compilation isn't necessarily wrong. Merely possible doesn't weaken.

questions.stimulus: Council member: Critics charge that the council acted improperly in approving the Fennell Road rezoning without first holding a public hearing. But the town charter requires a public hearing only for rezonings that substantially change the character of a neighborhood. And the Fennell Road rezoning made no such change, as is shown by the fact that the council, which always holds a hearing when the charter requires one, saw no need to hold a hearing on it.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the council member's argument is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that the argument
choices: confuses a condition that is required for a hearing to be mandatory with a condition that guarantees that a hearing is mandatory
takes for granted the correctness of the very judgment whose correctness the critics dispute
fails to consider that a rezoning might change a neighborhood's character in ways that are not substantial
rejects the critics' charge on the grounds that the critics have not proven that the rezoning changed the neighborhood's character
draws a general conclusion about the council's conduct on the basis of a single decision
questions.explanation: The critics dispute the council's judgment that no hearing was needed, yet the council member's only evidence that no hearing was needed is that the council judged none was needed; (B) identifies this circularity. (A) is the most tempting trap because the charter states a conditional, but the argument uses it correctly: a hearing is required only if the change is substantial, so if the change wasn't substantial, no hearing was required. (D) fails because the argument offers (circular) evidence of its own rather than relying on the critics' failure to prove their case.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The council acted properly in approving the rezoning without a hearing.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A hearing is required only if a rezoning substantially changes a neighborhood; this one didn't, because the council (which always holds required hearings) saw no need for one.

breakdown.analysis: How do we know the rezoning wasn't substantial? Because the council didn't hold a hearing. But whether the council was right not to hold a hearing is exactly what the critics are challenging. The member answers 'Was the council right?' with 'Yes, because the council decided so.' The conditional part is fine: Hearing required → substantial change. Contrapositive: no substantial change → no hearing required. That's valid. The trouble is the evidence for 'no substantial change,' which assumes the disputed decision was correct. It's like a referee saying 'that wasn't a foul, because I would have called it if it were.' Watch out: the formal-logic-looking answer is the trap here.

choices.note: Tempting, because there's an 'only' conditional in the stimulus. But the argument handles it correctly: substantial change is necessary for a required hearing, so no substantial change means no required hearing. No confusion.
choices.example: Example of flaw: A hearing is required only for substantial changes. This change is substantial, so a hearing was required.

choices.note: CORRECT. The critics say the council wrongly skipped a hearing. The member's proof that skipping was right is that the council skipped it. That assumes the disputed judgment was correct.
Irrelevant. Non-substantial changes don't trigger the charter, so overlooking them costs the argument nothing.
The member doesn't rely on the critics' lack of proof. He offers his own evidence (the council's judgment). That evidence is circular, but it's not an absence-of-evidence argument.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The critics haven't proven the neighborhood changed, so it didn't.

choices.note: The member draws no general conclusion about the council's conduct; he talks only about this rezoning. (He does mention the council 'always' holds required hearings, but that's a premise, not a conclusion drawn from one case.)
choices.example: Example of flaw: The council handled this rezoning well, so it handles every rezoning well.

questions.stimulus: Jolene Varga has proposed that the Tarrow Grain Cooperative require members to have their stored grain tested for mold before delivery after unusually wet harvests. But Varga apparently wants every load of grain sent to a laboratory year after year, no matter what the weather has been. A requirement like that would bankrupt the cooperative's smaller members, so her proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the argument is flawed because the argument
choices: fails to consider that laboratory testing for mold might cost less than the cooperative's smaller members expect
presumes that whatever would harm the cooperative's smaller members would also harm every other member of the cooperative
rejects Varga's proposal on the basis of her character rather than on the basis of the proposal's merits
presumes, without providing justification, that Varga wants grain tested every year regardless of the weather
takes for granted that unusually wet harvests occur too rarely to justify any testing requirement
questions.explanation: Straw man: Varga proposed testing only after unusually wet harvests, but the argument, with no justification, recasts her proposal as testing every load every year and attacks that. (D) describes the unsupported recasting. (A) is tempting because cost drives the objection, but even if lab tests were expensive, the objection still targets a proposal Varga never made.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Varga's proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Varga 'apparently' wants every load tested every year; that would bankrupt small members.

breakdown.analysis: Is that what Varga proposed? No. Her proposal is testing after unusually wet harvests. The argument swaps in a much bigger version (every load, every year, any weather) and knocks that down. That's a straw man. It's like someone suggesting you wear a coat when it snows, and you reply that wearing a coat every day of summer would be ridiculous. Prephrase: the argument attacks a distorted version of the proposal. Straw man is a classic; know it.

choices.note: Tempting, since cost is the stated objection. But the core problem isn't the price of a test. Even if testing were costly, the argument still attacks the wrong proposal.
The argument never says the requirement would harm every member, only that it would bankrupt the smaller ones. No part/whole move.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Small farms would suffer, so the whole co-op would suffer.

choices.note: Nothing is said about Varga's character. The argument attacks (a version of) the proposal, not the person.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Varga has never run a farm, so ignore her proposal.

choices.note: CORRECT. Varga proposed testing only after unusually wet harvests. The argument simply declares that she 'apparently' wants year-round testing of every load, offers no reason to think so, and then attacks that version.
The argument takes nothing for granted about how often wet harvests occur. If anything, it ignores the wet-harvest limit entirely.

questions.stimulus: The nurses' union at Halvern Hospital says that twelve-hour shifts cause fatigue-related errors, and it has proposed cutting back on their use. But eliminating twelve-hour shifts would leave the hospital's night units badly understaffed, since many nurses work nights only because a twelve-hour schedule lets them work three days a week. So the union's proposal should be rejected.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the argument?
choices: Many of the nurses who prefer twelve-hour shifts do so because they commute long distances to the hospital.
Fatigue-related errors are more common during the final hours of long shifts than during their first few hours.
Nurses who work on the hospital's night units are paid more per hour than nurses who work during the day.
Several other hospitals in the region have ended twelve-hour shifts within the past five years, citing nurses' fatigue.
The union proposes ending twelve-hour shifts only in intensive care, whose nurses do not staff the night units.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects the proposal because eliminating all twelve-hour shifts would understaff the night units, but (E) shows the union proposed something narrower that would not touch those night units, so the objection attacks a proposal the union didn't make. (B) is tempting because it supports the union's concern about fatigue, but it leaves the staffing objection untouched; (E) removes the basis of that objection.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The union's proposal should be rejected.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Ending twelve-hour shifts would understaff night units, because many night nurses rely on the three-day schedule.

breakdown.analysis: Is the argument attacking what the union actually proposed? The union proposed to 'cut back on their use,' but the argument attacks eliminating twelve-hour shifts altogether. If the proposal is narrower and doesn't touch the night units, the understaffing objection misses entirely. Prephrase: show that the proposal wouldn't affect the night units' schedules. It's like objecting to a ban on phones in the exam room by saying people need phones to call home: the ban doesn't cover the hallway. A great weakener here exposes a straw man.

choices.note: This explains why some nurses like long shifts, which if anything supports the staffing concern. Wrong direction.
Tempting: it backs the union's fatigue worry. But the argument never denied fatigue; its reason is staffing. This leaves that reason standing, so it only slightly helps the union.
Irrelevant. Night pay rates don't affect whether ending twelve-hour shifts would understaff night units.
So? Other hospitals' choices don't show this hospital's night units would be fine.
CORRECT. The proposal covers only intensive care, whose nurses don't staff the night units. So the night units wouldn't be understaffed, and the objection targets a proposal that wasn't made.

questions.stimulus: Some reporters at the Dunmore Herald have suggested that the paper skip its Monday print edition during the summer months, when advertising is scarce. But a newspaper that abandons its print edition gives up its most loyal readers, many of whom do not use the Internet at all. So the reporters' suggestion would be a serious mistake.
questions.stem: Which one of the following arguments exhibits a flawed pattern of reasoning most similar to that exhibited by the argument above?
choices: Some members have suggested that the gym close on Sundays. But Sunday is the gym's busiest day of the week, so closing then would cost the gym more revenue than closing on any other day. So the members' suggestion would be unwise.

Some residents have suggested that the town close its pool on Tuesdays in the off-season. But a town that closes its pool leaves children with no safe place to swim in summer. So the suggestion should be rejected.

Some residents have suggested that the town close its public pool on Tuesdays. But if the pool closes on Tuesdays, it will soon close on Wednesdays as well, and eventually it will close for good. So the residents' suggestion should be rejected.

Some residents have suggested that the town either keep its public pool open every day or close it permanently. Keeping it open every day would be too costly. So the town should close the pool permanently.

Some lifeguards have suggested that the town close its public pool on Tuesdays. But those lifeguards would enjoy an extra day off if the pool closed, so their suggestion should not be taken seriously.
questions.explanation: The argument rejects a modest suggestion (skip Monday editions in summer) by pointing to the bad results of a far more drastic one (abandoning print entirely): a straw man. (B) does the same, answering a proposal to close one off-season day with the harms of closing the pool altogether. (C) is the closest trap, but it predicts that the modest change will lead to the drastic one, a slippery-slope argument; it doesn't misdescribe the proposal itself.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The reporters' suggestion would be a serious mistake.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: A paper that abandons print loses its most loyal readers, many of whom aren't online.

setup.label: Pattern
setup.text: Someone suggests a limited cutback; the arguer cites the harm of a total cutback; so reject the suggestion.

breakdown.analysis: Who said anything about abandoning print? The reporters suggested skipping one day a week for a few months. The argument answers a different, much bigger proposal. Straw man. Prephrase: find an argument that rejects a limited proposal by citing the harms of an all-out version nobody proposed. Watch the look-alikes: slippery slope also ends at the extreme, but it gets there by predicting a chain of events, not by misdescribing the proposal.

choices.note: No distortion. The argument addresses exactly what was proposed (closing on Sundays) and gives a relevant reason against it. Not flawed in the same way.
CORRECT. A limited proposal (close Tuesdays in the off-season) is rejected by citing the harm of closing the pool altogether in summer: the same straw man as the Herald argument.
Tempting, since it also ends with the pool closing for good. But this is a slippery slope: it predicts the small change will snowball. It doesn't pretend the residents proposed closing for good.
choices.example: Example of flaw: If we let students retake one quiz, soon they'll demand to retake every exam.

choices.note: A false choice: two options presented as the only ones. The residents here really proposed those options, so there's no straw man.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Either we cancel the trip or we go in the rain; rain is miserable, so we must cancel.

choices.note: An attack on the proposers' motives (ad hominem), not a distortion of their proposal.
choices.example: Example of flaw: The reporters want Mondays off, so ignore their suggestion.

questions.stimulus: Columnist: Some consumer groups have urged the state to require that every household cleaning product list all of its chemical ingredients on its label. These groups evidently believe that ordinary shoppers can make sense of dozens of unfamiliar chemical names. But most shoppers cannot tell one chemical from another. So the groups' proposal rests on a false belief and should not be adopted.
questions.stem: Which one of the following is an assumption on which the columnist's argument depends?
choices: The case for the groups' proposal depends on most shoppers' being able to understand the chemical names on labels.
Most shoppers do not read the labels that household cleaning products currently carry before buying them.
The consumer groups have no evidence that any household cleaning product currently on the market is harmful.
The members of the consumer groups are themselves able to make sense of the chemical names on product labels.
Manufacturers would not change their products' formulas merely to avoid listing ingredients that shoppers might find alarming.
questions.explanation: The columnist attributes to the groups the belief that ordinary shoppers can interpret chemical names, refutes that belief, and rejects the proposal; this works only if the proposal really depends on that belief (labels could instead help allergy sufferers, doctors, or poison-control staff). (A) states that requirement, and negating it leaves the columnist attacking a position the proposal doesn't need. (E) is tempting because reformulation would be a benefit of labeling, but the argument never considers such benefits, so its negation adds a new reason for the proposal without breaking the columnist's chain of reasoning.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: The groups' labeling proposal rests on a false belief and should not be adopted.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: The groups evidently believe ordinary shoppers can make sense of chemical names; most shoppers can't tell one chemical from another.

breakdown.analysis: Does the proposal actually need shoppers to understand chemistry? Maybe not. A person with an allergy can look for one name. A doctor or poison-control worker can read the label after an accident. The columnist pins one rationale on the groups ('evidently'), knocks it down, and declares the whole proposal dead. That only works if the proposal stands or falls with that rationale. Prephrase: the proposal's justification depends on most shoppers understanding the names. Negation test: if the case doesn't depend on that, the columnist refuted a straw man.

choices.note: CORRECT. Negate it: the case for the proposal doesn't depend on most shoppers understanding the names. Then showing they can't understand them doesn't show the proposal rests on a false belief. The argument falls apart.
choices.negation: The case for the groups' proposal does not depend on most shoppers' being able to understand the chemical names on labels.

choices.note: Not needed. Whether shoppers read current labels is a different issue. Negating it doesn't touch the columnist's reasoning.
choices.negation: Most shoppers do read the labels that household cleaning products currently carry before buying them.

choices.note: The columnist's argument says nothing about evidence of harm. Negating it might help the groups in general, but it doesn't break the columnist's reasoning.
choices.negation: The consumer groups have some evidence that a household cleaning product currently on the market is harmful.

choices.note: Irrelevant. The proposal is about shoppers, not about what the groups' members can understand.
choices.negation: The members of the consumer groups are not themselves able to make sense of the chemical names on labels.

choices.note: Tempting, because reformulation would be a benefit of labeling the columnist ignores. But negating it just adds a new reason for the proposal; the columnist's chain (groups believe X; X is false; reject) isn't what it attacks. (A) is the link the argument actually needs.
choices.negation: Manufacturers would change their products' formulas to avoid listing ingredients that shoppers might find alarming.

questions.stimulus:
Ostrova: The observatory should stop letting a single committee made up entirely of senior staff decide which proposals receive time on its main telescope. Committees drawn from a single group tend to favor the kinds of projects that group already knows.

Haddad: Ostrova is mistaken. Our senior staff are among the most accomplished astronomers in the world, and many of the observatory's best-known discoveries came from projects they selected. There is no reason to think that less accomplished astronomers would choose better projects.
questions.stem: Haddad's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: presumes that astronomers who have made important discoveries are infallible judges of the proposals that other astronomers submit
takes for granted that the observatory's best-known discoveries are also the most scientifically important ones it has made
treats an objection to the committee's makeup as a proposal to staff it with less accomplished astronomers
concludes that the committee's past choices have been sound merely because no one has shown that they were unsound
draws a conclusion about all of the observatory's staff from the accomplishments of only its most senior members
questions.explanation: Ostrova objects that a committee drawn entirely from one group is too narrow; she never proposes swapping in less accomplished astronomers, yet Haddad's rebuttal argues against exactly that: a straw man (C). (A) is the most tempting trap, since Haddad leans on the staff's accomplishments, but he claims only that others would not choose better, not that the senior staff never err. (D) fails because Haddad cites positive evidence (past discoveries) rather than a mere lack of disproof.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: (Haddad) Ostrova is mistaken.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Senior staff are highly accomplished; many famous discoveries came from their picks; less accomplished astronomers wouldn't choose better.

breakdown.analysis: Did Ostrova say to put less accomplished people in charge? No. Her complaint is about composition: one group only, so the committee favors familiar projects. A mixed committee could still include senior staff, or outside astronomers just as accomplished. Haddad defends against a proposal Ostrova never made: replacing the experts with lesser ones. That's a straw man, a dialogue version where the second speaker answers a different, weaker position. It's like someone saying 'the hiring panel shouldn't be all engineers' and getting the reply 'our engineers are brilliant, and non-engineers wouldn't hire better.' Prephrase: Haddad misrepresents what Ostrova proposed.

choices.note: Tempting, since Haddad leans on the staff's track record. But he doesn't say they're infallible, only that lesser astronomers wouldn't do better. 'Infallible' overstates his claim.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Dr. Lee won a Nobel Prize, so every grant she approves must be worth funding.

choices.note: Haddad doesn't need or assume this. 'Best-known' discoveries are just his evidence that the staff picked well.
CORRECT. Ostrova objects to the committee's narrow makeup. Haddad treats that as if she wanted to hand the job to less accomplished astronomers, a position she never took.
Haddad offers positive evidence: discoveries from the projects they selected. He isn't relying on a lack of disproof.
choices.example: Example of flaw: No one has proven the committee made a bad choice, so all its choices were good.

choices.note: Haddad's claims are about the senior staff, who are the committee. He draws no conclusion about all staff.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Our senior astronomers are brilliant, so everyone who works at the observatory is brilliant.

sections.title: Flaw Patterns: Authority, Ad Hominem, Possible vs. Certain, Part vs. Whole

questions.stimulus: Renovation columnist: Delia Ormond, whose kitchen designs have won several national awards, recently advised homeowners not to install a vapor barrier when finishing a basement, saying that such barriers trap moisture inside the walls and encourage mold. Given Ormond's reputation, homeowners who are finishing their basements this year should follow her advice and leave the vapor barrier out.
questions.stem: The reasoning in the columnist's argument is flawed in that the argument
choices: draws a general conclusion about all basements from the experiences of a small number of homeowners in the area
presumes, without providing justification, that what is true of kitchens is also true of basements
attacks the motives of builders who routinely install vapor barriers rather than addressing the reasons they give
treats a person's expertise in one area as a reason to accept her advice in another
fails to consider that some homeowners may not be able to afford to finish their basements this year
questions.explanation: Bad authority: Ormond's awards are for kitchen design, but whether a vapor barrier traps moisture is a building-science question, so her reputation gives no real support to the advice. D says exactly this. B is the tempting trap because kitchens are mentioned, but the argument never reasons from kitchens to basements; kitchens only describe where Ormond's fame comes from.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Homeowners finishing basements this year should leave out the vapor barrier.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Delia Ormond, an award-winning kitchen designer, says vapor barriers trap moisture in basement walls.

breakdown.analysis: So what if she designs beautiful kitchens? Whether a vapor barrier traps moisture is a building-science question, not a design question. The columnist's only support is Ormond's reputation, and that reputation was earned somewhere else. It's like taking a famous pastry chef's word on how to rewire your fuse box. We need an answer that says the argument leans on an expert outside her field. This is the classic appeal to inappropriate authority. Know it.

choices.note: No sample here. The argument doesn't cite any homeowners' experiences at all. Its only evidence is one person's say-so.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Three of my neighbors skipped the vapor barrier and had no problems, so no basement needs one.

choices.note: Tempting, because kitchens come up. But kitchens only explain why Ormond is famous. The argument never says 'this works in kitchens, so it works in basements.'
choices.example: Example of flaw: Tile floors hold up well in kitchens, so they'll hold up well in basements too.

choices.note: The columnist never mentions builders, let alone their motives. That's ad hominem, and it isn't here.
choices.example: Example of flaw: Builders who install vapor barriers just want to pad their bills, so ignore what they say about moisture.

choices.note: CORRECT. Ormond's credentials are in kitchen design. The question is moisture control in basement walls. The argument treats her standing in one area as a reason to trust her in another, where it doesn't count.
Irrelevant. The advice is only for people who are finishing basements. Whether others can afford to doesn't touch the reasoning.

questions.stimulus: Winery owner: To win more medals for our white wines at the Larkmoor regional competition, we should age them in steel tanks rather than oak barrels. Teodor Vasko, who has judged at Larkmoor for twenty years, insists that steel-aged whites taste fresher and that the Larkmoor judges reward freshness above everything else. No one knows those judges' preferences better than Vasko, so switching to steel is clearly our best course.
questions.stem: Which one of the following, if true, most seriously weakens the winery owner's argument?
choices: Vasko has judged only red wines at Larkmoor, where white wines are scored by an entirely separate panel.
Some white wines aged in oak barrels have won top medals at several competitions other than Larkmoor.
Many people who regularly buy white wine say they prefer the flavor of whites aged in oak barrels.
Steel tanks cost considerably more to buy and install than the oak barrels the winery now uses.
The written guidelines given to Larkmoor judges list freshness alongside several other qualities that the judges are to consider.
questions.explanation: The plan rests entirely on Vasko's authority about what Larkmoor's judges reward. A shows his experience is with a different panel, so he has no special insight into how whites are scored, and the argument loses its only support. E is the tempting trap, but a list of several qualities is fully compatible with the judges caring about freshness most in practice.

setup.label: Conclusion
setup.text: Switching white-wine aging from oak to steel is the best way to win more Larkmoor medals.

setup.label: Reasoning
setup.text: Vasko, a Larkmoor judge for twenty years, says steel-aged whites taste fresher and that the judges reward freshness most; no one knows the judges better.

breakdown.analysis: Everything hangs on Vasko. Why should we believe him about how whites are judged? Because he's judged at Larkmoor for twenty years. But judged what, exactly? If his experience doesn't actually cover the white-wine panel, his 'insider knowledge' is just an opinion. We want an answer that cuts Vasko's expertise off from the specific question. Weakening an appeal to authority often works this way: you don't attack the claim, you show the authority isn't an authority on it.

choices.note: CORRECT. Vasko's twenty years are all on the red-wine side, and whites go to a different panel. So he has no special knowledge of what the white-wine judges reward, and the argument's only support collapses.
Other competitions are irrelevant. The argument is only about Larkmoor's judges.
Wrong group. The owner wants to please Larkmoor judges, not ordinary buyers.
Wrong dimension. The goal is medals, not saving money. A costly plan can still be the best way to win medals.
Tempting. It seems to dent 'above everything else.' But a guideline listing several qualities says nothing about which one the judges actually weight most. Freshness could still dominate in practice.

questions.stimulus: Some staff pharmacists at a regional hospital have objected that the hospital's new protocol for tapering patients off sedatives is too rapid and will cause withdrawal symptoms. In response, a hospital spokesperson noted that the protocol was reviewed and unanimously approved by the board of trustees, a group that includes several of the region's most accomplished business executives and attorneys, and concluded that the pharmacists' objection can be set aside.
questions.stem: The spokesperson's reasoning is most vulnerable to criticism on the grounds that it
choices: takes for granted that a tapering schedule that is rapid cannot also be safe for the patients who follow it
dismisses the pharmacists' objection on the grounds that pharmacists have a professional interest in how sedatives are prescribed
fails to consider that the protocol might produce side effects other than withdrawal symptoms in some patients
infers that the pharmacists' objection is false merely because it has not been shown to be true
